data.text/markdown:
Persistent homology of an image with phlite

We build the cubical complex of a greyscale image ourselves, as Python cells, attach the lower-star filtration (a cell appears with its brightest pixel), and read off the barcode and a representative loop for each ring in the image.
A 64 × 64 image: dark (low) pixels on three rings.

The cubical complex, as Python cells

Pixels are vertices; cells sit on a grid twice as fine, at (r, c): a vertex where both coordinates are even, an edge where one is odd, a square where both are. A cell's faces are one step either way along each odd coordinate. We describe cells as plain tuples and tell phlite how to get their dimension and boundary. Cells with equal values enter in the order they are listed, so every face must be listed before its cofaces: we list vertices, then edges, then squares.

The lower-star filtration

We only give values to the vertices (pixels); extend=True gives every other cell the largest value of its faces, which is exactly the lower-star filtration.

data.text/markdown: Three H1 bars stand out: the three rings, each born when its ring of dark pixels closes up and dying when its brighter centre fills in. Their representatives are loops of edges, which we can draw on the image (an edge between grid points (r, c) sits between the pixels at half those coordinates).

Watching the filtration

The sublevel set at time ||(t||) is every pixel darker than ||(t||) (with the edges and squares between them). As ||(t||) grows, components (H0) appear in the dark pixels and merge, and loops (H1) close up around each ring and are filled in when the brighter centre arrives. On the right, the bars alive at ||(t||) are highlighted.
